content: You were made alive when you were dead in transgressions and sins, {{v:2}} in which you once walked according to the course of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit who now works in the children of disobedience. {{v:3}} We also all once lived among them in the lusts of our flesh, doing the desires of the flesh and of the mind, and were by nature children of wrath, even as the rest. {{v:4}} But God, being rich in mercy, for his great love with which he loved us, {{v:5}} even when we were dead through our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ—by grace you have been saved— {{v:6}} and raised us up with him, and made us to sit with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus, {{v:7}} that in the ages to come he might show the exceeding riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus; {{v:8}} for by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, {{v:9}} not of works, that no one would boast. {{v:10}} For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared before that we would walk in them.

facets.text: Paul describes fallen humanity as spiritually dead in transgressions, not merely wounded or weakened. This death is a real incapacity, a life lived under the domination of sin, the world's course, and the demonic 'prince of the power of the air.' Because the condition is death, the remedy cannot come from within the sinner but only from God who alone gives life.
facets.question: What does it mean that we were spiritually dead before Christ?

facets.text: The passage names a threefold bondage from which we needed rescue: the world (the 'course of this world'), the devil (the 'prince of the power of the air'), and the flesh (the 'lusts of our flesh'). To be a 'child of disobedience' and 'by nature a child of wrath' is to share Adam's fallen state that precedes any individual choice. This diagnosis grounds the Church's teaching on original sin and the universal need for redemption.
facets.question: How does Scripture describe the powers that hold fallen humanity in bondage?

facets.text: The hinge of the whole passage is the phrase 'But God, being rich in mercy.' Human helplessness is answered not by human striving but by the initiative of divine love, which acts precisely 'when we were dead through our trespasses.' God's mercy is not a response to our worthiness but the free overflow of his love, revealing that salvation begins entirely on God's side.
facets.question: Why is God's mercy the true turning point of salvation?

facets.text: Paul unites the believer to Christ through three verbs mirroring Christ's own Paschal Mystery: made alive together with him, raised up with him, and seated with him in the heavenly places. Our redemption is not a separate transaction but an incorporation into Christ's death, resurrection, and ascension. What is true of the Head becomes, by grace, already true of the members even now.
facets.question: How are believers united to Christ's resurrection and ascension?

facets.text: Salvation is repeatedly declared to be 'by grace,' a gift of God 'not of yourselves' and 'not of works, that no one would boast.' This excludes any notion that a person earns redemption or that grace is a reward owed to human merit. The Catholic tradition receives this as the priority and gratuity of grace, which precedes, enables, and completes every human response of faith.
facets.question: Why is salvation a free gift and not something we earn?

facets.text: Faith is named as the means through which grace saves, yet even faith is called 'the gift of God.' Salvation is therefore neither a human achievement nor a bare mental assent but a graced relationship initiated by God. This preserves both the necessity of faith and its wholly gratuitous origin, guarding against both presumption and self-reliance.
facets.question: Is faith itself something God gives, or something we produce?

facets.text: Though works cannot earn salvation, Paul insists we are 'created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared before that we would walk in them.' Good works are not the cause of salvation but its intended fruit and goal. Grace does not abolish holy living; it creates it, so that the saved life necessarily unfolds in the good works God has appointed.
facets.question: If we are saved by grace, why do good works still matter?

facets.text: Paul calls the redeemed God's 'workmanship,' a new creation formed in Christ. Redemption is thus a fresh act of creation, restoring what sin had deadened and making the believer God's own handiwork. The ultimate purpose is doxological: 'in the ages to come' God will display 'the exceeding riches of his grace,' so that the whole drama of salvation exists to reveal and glorify God's kindness.
facets.question: What is the ultimate purpose of God saving us in Christ?

merged.annotation:
SUMMARY: Ephesians 2:1–10 moves from humanity's spiritual death under sin, the world, and the devil to salvation by God's free mercy, uniting believers to Christ's death, resurrection, and ascension, and forming them as a new creation for good works. Its doctrinal scope covers original sin, the gratuity of grace, faith as gift, and the place of works.

[DOCTRINAL | explicit]: Fallen humanity is spiritually dead in sin, an incapacity healed only by God who gives life, not by human effort.
[SCRIPTURAL | explicit]: A threefold bondage to the world, the devil ('prince of the power of the air'), and the flesh underlies the teaching on original sin and universal need for redemption.
[DOCTRINAL | explicit]: 'But God, rich in mercy' is the turning point; salvation begins wholly in God's free love while we were still dead in sin.
[TYPOLOGICAL | traditional]: Made alive, raised, and seated with Christ incorporates believers into his Paschal Mystery of death, resurrection, and ascension.
[DOCTRINAL | explicit]: Salvation is by grace, not works, so no one can boast or claim to have earned it—affirming grace's gratuity and priority.
[DOCTRINAL | explicit]: Faith is the means of salvation yet is itself God's gift, guarding against both presumption and self-reliance.
[MORAL | explicit]: Good works are the fruit and goal of grace, not its cause; the saved are created in Christ to walk in works God prepared.
[DEVOTIONAL | traditional]: The redeemed are God's 'workmanship,' a new creation, existing to display and glorify the riches of God's grace.
